The only time a person should be doing this "6 O'clock hold" is if their sights are calibrated for a further distance than the distance they are shooting. the bullet will land higher than where the sights are trained to.

If your weapon's sights are calibrated for 300 meters and you are shooting NATO rounds at 50 meters out you aim low.

Properly, you could (as it was taught by a damn good shooter/drill sergeant/sniper) imagine the tip of the front sight post as a dinner plate and the target resting on the plate. the bullet will make contact (if calibrated, say, for 100meters and shooting a 100meter target) like a pea sitting on that dinner plate.

if your pistol is calibrated for 50meters then aiming low at the target but not off the target is a good idea unless you are shooting a slow round and really need to aim even lower.. the nice thing about aiming for "6'clock" is you arent really off target,, just as low as possible.

and conversely if your pistol is set for around 25meters and you are shooting 60 meters out then 12 o clock would be a nice first shot maybe.

the front post is a dinner plate. the target needs to be like a pea on that plate. anything up or down is for elevation adjustment on the fly. if you calibrate your weapon for some arbitrary distance above the sight post you are doing it wrong.
